conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I want to review the plan for today—placing a gastrostomy tube to help with your hard-to-control low blood sugars after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Why do I need a tube again? I thought we were trying to avoid more surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The reason is your hypoglycemia has been medically refractory—despite diet changes and medications. Feeding into the stomach through a G-tube can sometimes stabilize sugars, and it also helps us see whether stomach feeding improves things enough to guide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this the same as reversing my bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—this is not a bypass reversal. This is a way to “temporize,” meaning help control symptoms now, and it can act like a test: if feeding through the stomach improves your blood sugars, it supports the idea that changing the bypass anatomy might help in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are the risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Risks include bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs, and problems with the tube like leakage or blockage. We do everything we can to minimize those. Anesthesia will also review their risks with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start you on a bariatric stage 5 diet when it’s safe, and we’ll add tube feeds when your bowels are ready. The tube feeds will be continuous at first to keep sugars steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of getting those shaky low sugar episodes again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood sugars closely here—before and after meals, at bedtime, and anytime you feel symptoms. If you feel shaky, sweaty, confused, or weak, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to head to the operating room. Any last questions before we go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… please tell me you’ll keep me comfortable after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll start with a pain pump right after surgery and then transition you to oral pain medicine as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi—surgery is done and you’re in recovery. We placed the gastrostomy tube. We also had to convert from laparoscopic to open surgery, and we repaired a small injury to the colon during the operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A colon injury? That sounds really bad. Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know that’s scary to hear. It was recognized right away and repaired during the same operation. We’ll watch you closely—your belly exam, your vital signs, and your labs—for any sign of a problem, but right now you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why it became an open surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Converting to open gives better exposure and lets us repair things safely. It’s not uncommon when anatomy is complex after prior surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach hurts a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a hydromorphone PCA—press the button when you need it. We’ll keep checking your pain and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Some nausea, and the incision feels tight. I’m afraid to move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That tightness is common after an open incision. Moving is important to prevent lung issues and blood clots. We’ll help you get up, use the incentive spirometer, and we’ll keep your pain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I stop the pain pump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll start transitioning—oral oxycodone for baseline pain, and IV hydromorphone only if you need breakthrough relief. The goal is to get you comfortable on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood sugars? Are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far they’ve been stable with close monitoring. We’ll keep checking frequently, especially as we adjust diet and start tube feeds later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m checking in because your abdomen looks more distended today. Have you passed gas or had a bowel movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I feel bloated and uncomfortable. Is something wrong with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This can happen after abdominal surgery—your intestines can temporarily “go to sleep,” called an ileus. We’re going to get an abdominal x-ray to look for ileus and to make sure there’s no free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray tech said they couldn’t see the tube tip well. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray shows an ileus—gas in the bowel consistent with things being slow—and no free air. The tube is seen over the left abdomen, but the exact tip isn’t well visualized on this type of film. Clinically the tube site looks fine, and we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do we do for the ileus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mainly supportive care: walking, minimizing narcotics as we can, and time. We can try a suppository to help stimulate things, but sometimes it takes a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repeated the abdominal x-ray this afternoon. It still looks like a post-operative ileus, and the contrast hasn’t moved much yet. Importantly, there’s still no sign of free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a leak from the colon repair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s nothing suggesting a leak—your exam and imaging don’t show free air, and we’re watching your temperature and labs closely. If you develop worsening pain, fever, or new tenderness, we’d reassess immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning? Any flatus yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no. I’m frustrated. And my heart feels like it’s racing sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some intermittent tachycardia—faster heart rate—but you’ve been stable and not having chest pain or shortness of breath. Pain, dehydration, and the stress of surgery can contribute. We’ll keep monitoring and make sure you’re well hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink more? My mouth is so dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance sips with your belly distention. We’ll also keep IV fluids going as needed while the ileus improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your abdomen looks less distended today. Have you passed gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, yes. And I had a tiny bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign the ileus is resolving. Today we can start tube feedings slowly and advance as you tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of formula is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A high-protein, moderate-carbohydrate formula—about 45% carbohydrate. The goal is steady delivery to help prevent big swings in blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel sick when it starts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some fullness. We’ll start at a low rate, check for nausea, distention, diarrhea, and we’ll check residuals as instructed. If you feel worse, we slow down or pause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeding is running. I’m worried it will make my sugars drop like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching your glucose closely. Continuous feeding tends to smooth out the peaks and dips. If you feel symptoms—shaky, sweaty, lightheaded—tell us immediately and we’ll check a fingerstick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight with the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than I expected. No vomiting. Some cramping but not too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll continue to advance toward the goal rate as long as your belly stays soft and you’re not getting distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my incision and the tube site—how do I take care of it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll teach you. For the tube site: wash gently with mild soap and water. Keep a dressing if there’s drainage; once it’s dry, you can leave it open. For the incision, keep it clean and watch for redness, swelling, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the tube clogs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll flush it with water on schedule—at home it will be 100 mL free water every 8 hours. If you can’t flush or the feeding won’t run, stop and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you’re at the goal tube feed rate and tolerating it. Your blood sugars have been stable on this regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the hypoglycemia is fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we’ve found a way to control it right now. The underlying issue—what we’ve been calling nesidioblastosis—can still cause episodes, so you’ll continue frequent glucose checks and follow up closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still taking my acarbose and pramlintide, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll resume your regular home medications unless we specifically tell you otherwise. Your discharge list includes acarbose with meals and pramlintide with meals, along with your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about constipation with the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good concern. You’ll have docusate twice daily, and bisacodyl as needed. Also walking and fluids help. We’ll aim to keep the oxycodone only as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I shower? And do I need to keep a dressing on the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can wash around the tube with mild soap and water. If there’s no drainage, you can omit the dressing. If you notice new drainage, redness, or worsening pain, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge planning day. You’re afebrile, walking independently, tolerating bariatric stage 5 diet plus continuous tube feeds, and your pain is controlled on oral medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going home with the feeding pump running all day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continuous 24 hours per day for now: Replete with Fiber at 55 mL per hour. You’ll flush with 100 mL water every 8 hours. Home services will help with supplies and teaching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What symptoms mean I should stop the feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop significant abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, worsening abdominal pain, or high residuals when you aspirate the tube—especially more than 50 mL—stop the feeding and call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I check residuals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use a 60 mL syringe to aspirate from the tube before feeding. If you pull back more than 50 mL, hold the feeding and notify the physician who ordered the formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar checks—how often at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Routinely before and after meals, at bedtime, and any time you feel symptoms. If you have trouble tolerating feeds or tube issues, check even more closely and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about fever? I’m scared of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have shaking chills or a fever over 101.5°F, or if the incision or tube site becomes red, swollen, draining, or increasingly painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special because of the colon repair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main thing is to watch for concerning symptoms—worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, or inability to pass gas or stool again. You’ve been doing well, and we didn’t see signs of infection during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. This tube feeding plan is meant to keep you stable while you follow up with the specialists who’ve been evaluating your hypoglycemia. We’ll make sure you leave with clear instructions and contacts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’ll continue your home meds, plus omeprazole twice daily, liquid oxycodone as needed, and the bowel regimen. You’re set up for home services for the tube feeding. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just please make sure I have the number to call if the tube leaks or my sugars drop.
